ap_cardiovascular.title: Heart, blood flow, and blood vessels
ap_cardiovascular.intro_markdown: The heart is a double pump moving blood through two circuits. Deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium from the body, passes the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, and is pumped through the pulmonary valve to the lungs for oxygen. Oxygenated blood returns to the left atrium, crosses the mitral (bicuspid) valve into the left ventricle, and exits through the aortic valve to the body. Valves keep blood flowing one way, and vessels specialize: arteries carry blood away from the heart (usually oxygenated, except the pulmonary arteries), while veins return blood to the heart (usually deoxygenated, except the pulmonary veins). Worked example: the left ventricle has the thickest wall because it must generate enough pressure to push blood through the entire systemic circuit.
key_points: Trace the pathway: vena cava → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary valve → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → mitral valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta → body.
Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry blood toward it — the pulmonary vessels are the exception.
Valves prevent backflow: atrioventricular (tricuspid, mitral) and semilunar (pulmonary, aortic) valves keep blood moving one direction.
The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pumps against the highest pressure in the systemic circuit.
The SA node is the heart's pacemaker; veins hold most blood volume, and capillaries are the exchange sites.

items.stem: Which valve is located between the right atrium and the right ventricle?
items.rationale: The tricuspid valve (three cusps) sits between the right atrium and right ventricle, allowing one-way flow of deoxygenated blood entering the heart from the body.
distractor_rationales: The mitral valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle, not on the right side.
Correct: the tricuspid valve separates the right atrium from the right ventricle.
The pulmonary valve is a semilunar valve at the exit of the right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk.
The aortic valve is a semilunar valve at the exit of the left ventricle into the aorta.

items.stem: Which vessels carry deoxygenated blood back to the heart from the body tissues?
items.rationale: Veins carry blood toward the heart. Systemic veins return deoxygenated blood from body tissues, unlike pulmonary veins, which carry oxygenated blood to the heart.
distractor_rationales: The pulmonary arteries are exceptions: they carry deoxygenated blood away from the heart to the lungs.
Arterioles regulate blood flow but are still arteries and carry blood away from the heart.
Correct: veins return blood toward the heart, and systemic veins carry deoxygenated blood.
Capillaries are exchange vessels, not the vessels that return blood to the heart.

items.stem: In which vessels does the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide with body tissues occur?
items.rationale: Capillaries have walls only one cell thick, allowing rapid diffusion of oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrients, and wastes between blood and tissue cells.
distractor_rationales: Correct: gas exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide occurs across capillary walls.
The aorta is a large artery conducting blood away from the heart; no gas exchange occurs there.
The venae cavae return deoxygenated blood to the right atrium without exchange.
The left ventricle is a pump chamber, not an exchange site.

llm_review.issues: Option 4 is a heart chamber, not a vessel, making it easier to eliminate; otherwise the item is sound.

items.stem: Which heart chamber has the thickest myocardium, and why?
items.rationale: The left ventricle pumps blood through the entire systemic circulation, requiring the highest pressure, so it has the thickest muscular wall of any chamber.
distractor_rationales: The right atrium receives blood and is thin-walled because it fills under low pressure.
The right ventricle only pumps to the nearby lungs, so its wall is thinner than the left ventricle.
The left atrium fills under low pressure from the pulmonary veins and has a relatively thin wall.
Correct: the left ventricle must generate enough pressure to drive blood through the whole systemic circuit, so it is the most muscular chamber.

llm_review.issues: Stem asks 'and why?' but options list only chambers; the rationale supplies the reason, so the 'why' is not part of the answer choices.

items.stem: What event produces the second heart sound (the 'dub') heard during auscultation?
options: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves
items.rationale: The 'dub' (S2) occurs when the aortic and pulmonary semilunar valves snap shut at the beginning of ventricular diastole, preventing backflow into the ventricles.
distractor_rationales: The mitral valve is on the left side of the heart, between the left atrium and left ventricle.
The tricuspid valve separates the right atrium from the right ventricle and is not heard at the second intercostal space.
Correct: the second heart sound (S2, the 'dub') is closure of the aortic and pulmonary semilunar valves at the start of ventricular relaxation.
The superior vena cava is a vessel, not a valve, and plays no role in heart sounds.

items.stem: Which structure is known as the heart's pacemaker because it normally initiates each heartbeat?
items.rationale: The SA node, located in the wall of the right atrium, depolarizes spontaneously about 60-100 times per minute, making it the heart's natural pacemaker that sets normal sinus rhythm.
distractor_rationales: The AV node delays the impulse only briefly (about 0.1 s) before relaying it to the ventricles; it is not the primary pacemaker.
Correct: the SA node in the right atrium normally initiates each heartbeat at 60-100 times per minute, setting the pace for the heart.
The bundle of His conducts the impulse from the atria to the ventricles but does not originate it.
Purkinje fibers distribute the impulse through the ventricular myocardium for contraction but do not set the resting rhythm.

items.stem: A patient's blood sample is drawn from a vessel entering the left atrium. What is the expected oxygen content of this blood?
items.rationale: In the pulmonary circuit, gas exchange reverses the usual pattern: the pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium, making them the exception among veins.
distractor_rationales: Correct: the pulmonary veins are the only veins carrying oxygenated blood, returning it from the lungs to the left atrium.
Systemic veins carry deoxygenated blood from body tissues to the right atrium.
The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood away from the heart to the lungs.
The superior vena cava returns deoxygenated blood from the upper body to the right atrium.

items.stem: A patient has a damaged mitral valve that fails to close completely. During ventricular systole, in which direction will blood flow abnormally?
options: From the right ventricle into the right atrium
From the left ventricle into the right atrium
From the left atrium into the right ventricle
From the left ventricle into the left atrium
items.rationale: The mitral valve normally closes during ventricular systole. If it fails, high left ventricular pressure drives blood backward into the left atrium, causing regurgitation and reduced cardiac output.
distractor_rationales: The tricuspid valve guards the right atrioventricular opening, not the left.
Blood regurgitates into the left atrium, not the right atrium, when the mitral valve fails.
The right ventricle pumps to the lungs and is not involved in mitral valve incompetence.
Correct: failure of the mitral valve to close fully lets blood regurgitate from the left ventricle into the left atrium during systole, producing a murmur and reducing forward output.

llm_review.issues: Distractors 2 and 3 are anatomically implausible, so the item has limited discrimination.

ap_cells_tissues.title: Cells, tissues, and homeostasis
ap_cells_tissues.intro_markdown: Cells are the body's basic units of structure and function. Each contains organelles with specialized jobs: mitochondria make ATP, ribosomes build proteins, the Golgi apparatus packages and ships them, and lysosomes digest worn-out material. Cells organize into four tissue types: epithelial tissue covers and lines surfaces, connective tissue binds and supports with a nonliving matrix, muscle tissue contracts, and nervous tissue sends electrical signals. Homeostasis keeps the body's internal conditions near a set point through negative feedback: a sensor detects a change, a control center compares it to the set point, and an effector produces a response that pushes the variable back toward normal. Water also moves across cell membranes by osmosis toward the more concentrated (solute-rich) solution. Worked example: a red blood cell placed in 5% salt water sits in a solution more concentrated than its interior, so water leaves the cell and it shrinks and creases; placed in distilled water, water floods in and the cell swells and may burst.
key_points: Mitochondria produce most cellular ATP; ribosomes synthesize proteins; lysosomes digest wastes; the Golgi apparatus packages and ships proteins.
The four tissue types are epithelial (covering/lining), connective (support with matrix), muscle (contraction), and nervous (signaling).
Negative feedback reverses a change and returns a variable toward its set point; it is the main mechanism of homeostasis.
Osmosis moves water toward the more concentrated solution: hypertonic surroundings shrink a cell, hypotonic surroundings swell it.
Secreted proteins travel from rough ER to the Golgi apparatus to secretory vesicles for release by exocytosis.

items.stem: A skeletal muscle cell performs vigorous contraction and needs a large continuous supply of ATP. Which organelle produces most of this ATP?
items.rationale: Mitochondria carry out aerobic cellular respiration, producing most of the ATP that powers muscle contraction; the other organelles make, digest, or package proteins instead of energy.
distractor_rationales: Correct: mitochondria perform aerobic respiration, converting nutrient energy into ATP, the main energy currency for contracting muscle cells.
Ribosomes synthesize proteins, including the contractile proteins themselves, but they do not generate ATP.
Lysosomes digest wastes and damaged organelles; they do not produce usable energy.
The Golgi apparatus modifies and packages proteins for secretion; it is a shipping station, not a power plant.

items.stem: Which tissue type forms continuous sheets that cover body surfaces and line internal cavities and hollow organs?
items.rationale: Epithelial tissue forms continuous sheets that cover body surfaces, line cavities and vessels, and make up glands; its cells are tightly packed with little matrix between them.
distractor_rationales: Connective tissue binds and supports structures through a matrix, as in bone and fat; it does not cover free surfaces.
Muscle tissue generates force through contraction; it is specialized for movement, not lining.
Correct: epithelial tissue forms sheets that cover surfaces and line cavities, with one free surface exposed to the lumen or outside.
Nervous tissue transmits electrical signals for communication and control; it does not form covering sheets.

items.stem: During exercise, core body temperature rises above its set point. Which response best illustrates the negative feedback mechanism that returns temperature toward normal?
options: Skin blood vessels constrict and skeletal muscles begin shivering
Sweat glands increase secretion and skin blood vessels dilate
The hypothalamic set point resets to a higher temperature
Thyroid hormone secretion increases to raise metabolic heat production
items.rationale: Rising temperature triggers heat-loss responses: sweating and cutaneous vasodilation. Because the response reverses the original change, this is negative feedback holding temperature near its set point.
distractor_rationales: Constricting skin vessels and shivering are responses to cold, not heat; they would raise body temperature further.
Correct: sweating with dilation of skin blood vessels increases heat loss, lowering body temperature toward the set point, which defines negative feedback.
A negative feedback system does not reset its set point upward; that describes fever pathology, not the normal heat-loss response.
Increasing metabolic heat production would drive temperature higher and is the opposite of the needed correction.

items.stem: A red blood cell is placed in a solution that has a higher solute concentration than the cell's interior. What happens to the cell?
options: Swells and may burst as water enters by osmosis
Shows no net water movement because the membrane is impermeable to water
Pumps water out using active transport proteins
Shrinks and crenates as water leaves by osmosis
items.rationale: The fluid is hypertonic: its solute concentration exceeds the cell's, so water moves out of the cell by osmosis and the cell shrinks with a scalloped (crenated) edge.
distractor_rationales: Swelling and bursting occur in a hypotonic solution, where the outside is less concentrated and water enters the cell.
The concentration difference across the membrane creates a large osmotic driving force, so net water movement definitely occurs.
Water crosses membranes by osmosis through the lipid bilayer and aquaporins; no ATP is spent, so this is not active transport.
Correct: in a hypertonic environment water follows its gradient and leaves the cell, causing the cell to shrink and crenate.

items.stem: In a dividing cell, during which stage of mitosis do sister chromatids separate and are pulled toward opposite poles of the spindle?
options: Sister chromatids separate and move toward opposite spindle poles
Chromosomes first condense and the nuclear envelope breaks down
Chromosomes align along the cell's equatorial plane
Two new nuclear envelopes form around separated chromosomes
items.rationale: Anaphase is the separation stage: cohesion proteins break down, sister chromatids split, and motor activity moves them along spindle microtubules to opposite poles of the cell.
distractor_rationales: Correct: anaphase is defined by the splitting of sister chromatids and their migration along spindle fibers toward the spindle poles.
Prophase is marked by chromatin condensing into visible chromosomes and breakdown of the nuclear envelope; chromatids have not yet separated.
Metaphase features chromosomes aligned on the cell's equatorial plate, still fully attached and unseparated.
Telophase occurs after separation: nuclear envelopes reform around the two new sets of chromosomes, which then decondense.

llm_review.issues: Options are descriptions rather than stage names, though option 1 correctly describes anaphase.

items.stem: Blood is classified as a connective tissue. What feature justifies this classification?
options: Because its cells contain contractile proteins that shorten
Because its cells conduct electrical impulses to target organs
Because it completely lacks any matrix between its cells
Because its cells are suspended in a nonliving liquid matrix
items.rationale: Connective tissue is defined by widely separated cells within a nonliving extracellular matrix. In blood, that matrix is liquid plasma suspending erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets.
distractor_rationales: Blood cells are not contractile; force production belongs to muscle tissue, which is never classified as blood.
Conducting electrical impulses is the defining property of nervous tissue, not of the cells suspended in plasma.
Blood has an abundant matrix: the liquid plasma, which is exactly why it fits the connective category.
Correct: connective tissues consist of cells separated by a nonliving matrix, and blood's matrix is the liquid plasma suspending its cells.

items.stem: After a meal, blood glucose rises above its set range. Pancreatic beta cells detect the increase and secrete insulin, which signals liver, muscle, and fat cells to remove glucose from the blood. In this negative feedback loop, which component is the effector?
options: The elevated blood glucose concentration itself
Liver, muscle, and adipose cells that take up glucose from the blood
The insulin receptor, which resets to a new glucose set point
The beta cells of the pancreatic islets
items.rationale: Beta cells sense the high glucose and release insulin (sensor/control center); insulin's target cells in liver, muscle, and fat are the effectors, taking up glucose and lowering blood levels back toward the set point.
distractor_rationales: The elevated glucose is the stimulus, the variable being monitored, not the structure that carries out the response.
Correct: effectors are the components that produce the correcting response; liver, muscle, and fat cells take up glucose and lower the blood level, closing the loop.
Negative feedback loops operate around a fixed set point; there is no adjustable receptor set point resetting here.
Pancreatic beta cells act as the sensor and control center, detecting glucose and releasing insulin, but they do not remove glucose from the blood themselves.

llm_review.issues: Option 3 is a weak distractor because an insulin receptor does not reset the glucose set point; otherwise the item is physiologically sound and has a clear best answer.

items.stem: A pancreatic cell makes a digestive enzyme that will be released into a duct. Which sequence correctly traces this protein from synthesis to secretion?
options: Golgi apparatus, then rough ER, then a transport vesicle fusing with the plasma membrane
Free ribosome in the cytosol, then a lysosome, then exocytosis at the plasma membrane
Ribosome on the rough ER, then the Golgi apparatus, then a secretory vesicle that fuses with the plasma membrane
Ribosome on the rough ER, then a lysosome, then diffusion of the protein directly through the plasma membrane
items.rationale: Secreted proteins follow the endomembrane route: translation on a rough ER ribosome, folding and modification in the ER lumen, further processing and packaging in the Golgi, then vesicular export by exocytosis.
distractor_rationales: This order puts the Golgi before the rough ER, but newly made proteins travel from the ER to the Golgi, not the reverse.
Ribosomes bound to the rough ER synthesize secreted proteins; free ribosomes in the cytosol make proteins that stay inside the cell.
Correct: the polypeptide is made on a bound ribosome, threaded into the rough ER, modified in the Golgi, packaged into a vesicle, and released by exocytosis.
Lysosomes digest and recycle material; secreted proteins are never routed through lysosomes, which would destroy them.

llm_review.issues: No significant content issue; option 3 is the only correct endomembrane secretion pathway. Some distractors are less plausible than others.

ap_digestive_urinary.title: Digestive and urinary systems
ap_digestive_urinary.intro_markdown: The digestive system breaks food into absorbable units and the urinary system filters blood to maintain fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance. In the digestive tract, mechanical work (chewing, churning, peristalsis) moves and mixes food, while enzymes chemically split starches, proteins, and fats. Most nutrient absorption happens in the small intestine, whose villi and microvilli create an enormous surface area. Accessory organs assist without touching the food path: the liver makes bile, the gallbladder stores it, and the pancreas supplies digestive enzymes and buffers. In the kidney, roughly 1.2 million nephrons per organ filter plasma at the glomerulus, and about 99% of that filtrate is reabsorbed — most of it in the proximal convoluted tubule. Hormones fine-tune the remainder: ADH lets the collecting duct reabsorb water, and aldosterone promotes sodium reabsorption with potassium secretion. Worked example: at a GFR of 125 mL/min, one hour produces 7,500 mL of filtrate; if 99% is reabsorbed, urine output is 75 mL/hr.
key_points: Salivary amylase begins starch digestion; the stomach's pepsin begins protein digestion; pancreatic lipase digests fat.
The liver produces bile and the gallbladder stores it; bile emulsifies fat but does not chemically digest it.
Villi and microvilli give the small intestine its huge absorptive surface; most nutrients enter blood there, fats enter lacteals.
The nephron is the kidney's functional unit; the proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs about 65% of filtrate, and only about 1% of filtrate leaves as urine.
ADH increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct; aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion, raising blood volume and pressure.

items.stem: Saliva contains an enzyme that begins the chemical digestion of food in the mouth. Which nutrient does this enzyme act on?
items.rationale: Salivary amylase chemically digests starch into smaller sugars such as maltose. Its action continues briefly in the stomach before gastric acid inactivates it.
distractor_rationales: Salivary amylase hydrolyzes starch into maltose and shorter polysaccharides, so carbohydrate is the nutrient targeted.
Protein digestion begins in the stomach with pepsin, not in saliva.
Lipid digestion begins in the small intestine with pancreatic lipase; bile only emulsifies fat.
Vitamins require no enzymatic digestion because they are absorbed as intact molecules.

items.stem: Which accessory organ of digestion produces bile?
items.rationale: The liver's hepatocytes produce bile, which the gallbladder then stores and concentrates before releasing it into the duodenum.
distractor_rationales: The pancreas supplies digestive enzymes and bicarbonate to the small intestine but does not synthesize bile.
Hepatocytes continually produce bile from cholesterol and bilirubin; bile then flows toward the gallbladder for storage.
The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile but produces none of it.
The stomach produces hydrochloric acid and pepsinogen, not bile.

items.stem: A bolus of food is moved from the esophagus toward the stomach by waves of alternating smooth muscle contraction and relaxation. This process is called:
items.rationale: Peristalsis consists of rhythmic waves of smooth muscle contraction behind the bolus and relaxation ahead of it, propelling food along the tract.
distractor_rationales: Diffusion is passive molecular movement across membranes and plays no role in propelling food.
Absorption is the transfer of digested nutrients into blood or lymph, not a movement pattern.
Peristalsis is the alternating waves of smooth muscle contraction and relaxation that push a bolus forward.
Emulsification is the breakdown of fat globules by bile salts, a chemical process rather than propulsion.

items.stem: Most nutrient absorption in the digestive tract occurs in the small intestine. Which structures account for the enormous absorptive surface area of its lining?
items.rationale: Villi are fingerlike mucosal folds covered by microvilli (brush border). Together they multiply surface area hundreds of fold and house the absorbing epithelial cells.
distractor_rationales: Gastric pits are indentations in the stomach lining that secrete acid and mucus; the stomach absorbs little besides alcohol and some drugs.
Haustra are pouches of the large intestine formed by its muscle bands; they aid water reabsorption, not nutrient absorption.
Intestinal crypts secrete intestinal juice and harbor stem cells; absorption occurs above them at the villous surface.
Villi and microvilli massively expand the mucosal surface area, and their epithelial cells transfer nutrients into capillaries and lacteals.

items.stem: Of the roughly 180 liters of filtrate formed each day, about 99% is reabsorbed. In which nephron segment does the largest fraction of this reabsorption occur?
options: Descending limb of the loop of Henle
items.rationale: The PCT, with its brush border and abundant transporters, reabsorbs about two thirds of filtrate water and solutes, including essentially all filtered glucose and amino acids.
distractor_rationales: The PCT reabsorbs roughly 65% of the filtrate, including virtually all glucose and amino acids and most water and salts.
The distal convoluted tubule fine-tunes only about 5% of sodium and water under hormonal control.
The collecting duct adjusts final water recovery under ADH; it reabsorbs a smaller fraction of filtrate.
The descending limb of the loop of Henle is permeable to water but reabsorbs less filtrate than the PCT.

items.stem: A patient is dehydrated, and the posterior pituitary releases antidiuretic hormone (ADH). What is ADH's primary effect on the kidney?
options: The glomerulus, where it increases filtration rate
The collecting duct, where it increases water reabsorption
The proximal tubule, where it increases sodium reabsorption
The bladder, where it increases storage capacity
items.rationale: Dehydration raises ADH (vasopressin), which inserts aquaporin water channels into collecting duct cells, so more water returns to blood and urine becomes concentrated.
distractor_rationales: ADH does not act on the glomerulus, and GFR is regulated mainly by renal autoregulation, sympathetic tone, and angiotensin II.
ADH prompts insertion of aquaporins in the collecting duct, increasing water reabsorption and concentrating urine.
Sodium reabsorption in the nephron is governed chiefly by aldosterone acting on the distal tubule and collecting duct, not ADH.
The bladder is a storage reservoir with no role in ADH-mediated water recovery.

items.stem: A patient's glomerular filtration rate is 125 mL/min. Assuming 99% of the filtrate is reabsorbed, approximately how much urine does this patient produce per hour?
items.rationale: 125 mL/min × 60 = 7,500 mL of filtrate per hour. If 99% is reabsorbed, 1% remains: 7,500 × 0.01 = 75 mL of urine per hour.
distractor_rationales: This is the total filtrate volume formed per hour; it ignores that about 99% is reabsorbed.
This answer applies 90% reabsorption instead of 99%, a tenfold overestimate.
Correct: 125 mL/min × 60 min = 7,500 mL of filtrate; 1% remaining = 75 mL of urine per hour.
This answer removed 99.9% of the filtrate rather than 99%, misplacing the decimal by one place.

items.stem: A patient's blood pressure falls. The kidneys release renin, and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system is activated. What is aldosterone's effect on the kidney?
options: Increases sodium excretion in the urine
Increases water excretion without changing electrolytes
Increases sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion
items.rationale: Aldosterone acts on the distal tubule and collecting duct to reabsorb Na+ (with water following) and secrete K+, raising blood volume and pressure.
distractor_rationales: Aldosterone does the opposite: it conserves sodium, which is why excess aldosterone causes sodium retention and edema.
Aldosterone's water retention follows passively from sodium reabsorption; it does not directly alter urine volume without electrolyte change.
Aldosterone does not directly change GFR; its renal effects are on tubular sodium and potassium transport.
Aldosterone upregulates sodium-potassium pumps and channels in the distal tubule and collecting duct, sparing Na+ and water while increasing K+ loss in urine.

ap_nervous_endocrine.title: Nervous and endocrine systems
ap_nervous_endocrine.intro_markdown: The nervous and endocrine systems are the body's two great communication networks, and they work together to keep conditions inside the body stable (homeostasis). The **nervous system** sends fast electrical signals along neurons: dendrites receive input, the axon carries the action potential, and synapses pass the message chemically via neurotransmitters. Structurally it divides into the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and peripheral nervous system (somatic "voluntary" and autonomic "involuntary" branches). The **endocrine system** is slower but longer-lasting: glands release hormones into the blood, and only cells with matching receptors respond. The hypothalamus links the two systems: it runs the pituitary gland, the "master gland" whose hormones control other glands through feedback loops. Worked example: when blood calcium runs low, the parathyroid glands release parathyroid hormone, which raises calcium back toward normal; when calcium is high, a negative feedback loop shuts the hormone off.
key_points: Axons carry impulses away from the neuron's cell body; dendrites carry signals toward it.
The nervous system acts fast with electrical signals; the endocrine system acts slower but longer with hormones in the blood.
The sympathetic division prepares for 'fight or flight'; the parasympathetic division promotes 'rest and digest'.
The hypothalamus controls the pituitary; negative feedback loops keep hormone levels stable.
Parathyroid hormone raises blood calcium; calcitonin from the thyroid lowers it.
The sodium-potassium pump moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP, maintaining the resting membrane potential.

items.stem: Which part of a neuron carries nerve impulses away from the cell body?
items.rationale: Axons conduct nerve impulses away from the cell body toward the synaptic terminals; dendrites carry signals toward the cell body.
distractor_rationales: Correct: axons are the neuron fibers specialized to conduct impulses away from the cell body toward the terminal.
Dendrites receive signals and carry them toward the cell body, not away from it.
The soma (cell body) houses the nucleus and maintains the neuron but does not conduct impulses.
Myelin is an insulating sheath made by glial cells, not the conducting fiber itself.

items.stem: What is the defining feature of an endocrine gland?
options: Glands that secrete through ducts onto body surfaces
Glands that release waste products into the urine
Ductless glands that release hormones into the bloodstream
Glands that transmit electrical impulses to target cells
items.rationale: Endocrine glands are ductless and secrete hormones into the blood, which carries them to distant cells with specific receptors.
distractor_rationales: These glands secrete directly into ducts, which defines exocrine glands, not endocrine ones.
Hormones act only on cells bearing the matching receptor, so not every cell is a target.
Correct: ductless glands releasing hormones into the bloodstream to act on target cells with receptors define the endocrine system.
Neurons communicate by neurotransmitters across synapses, while endocrine glands broadcast hormones via blood.

llm_review.issues: Option 2 is a weak distractor; option 1 is the main plausible misconception, while option 4 tests neural vs endocrine signaling.

items.stem: After a frightening event passes, which division of the autonomic nervous system slows the heart rate and promotes digestion?
items.rationale: The parasympathetic division dominates during rest, promoting 'rest and digest' activities such as a decreased heart rate and increased digestion.
distractor_rationales: The sympathetic division is the 'fight or flight' system, and it typically increases heart rate.
Correct: the parasympathetic division is the 'rest and digest' system, conserving energy and slowing the heart.
The somatic system controls voluntary skeletal muscle movement, not involuntary heart rate.
The enteric division manages the digestive tract and does not slow the heart rate.

items.stem: Blood calcium drops below the normal range. Which hormone is released to raise it back toward normal?
items.rationale: Low blood calcium triggers the parathyroid glands to release parathyroid hormone, which raises calcium by acting on bone, kidneys, and the gut.
distractor_rationales: Thyroid-stimulating hormone is released by the anterior pituitary to act on the thyroid, not by the thyroid itself.
Calcitonin helps lower blood calcium, which is the opposite of the needed effect here.
Aldosterone is an adrenal cortex hormone that regulates sodium and water balance, not blood calcium.
Correct: parathyroid hormone raises blood calcium by stimulating bone breakdown and calcium reabsorption in the kidneys.

items.stem: A stroke damages motor areas of the left cerebral cortex. Where would weakness most likely appear?
options: Weakness on the left side of the body
Weakness on the right side of the body
No motor effects because impulses stay on the same side
Weakness of both sides from spinal reflexes
items.rationale: Motor fibers from the left cerebral hemisphere cross (decussate) in the medulla, so a left-hemisphere stroke produces weakness on the right side of the body.
distractor_rationales: The left hemisphere receives sensory input from the right side of the body, so this reversal points to a crossed pathway.
Correct: corticospinal tracts decussate in the medulla oblongata, so a left-hemisphere stroke typically causes right-sided weakness.
Impulses actually cross; describing them as staying on the same side is the misconception being tested.
Spinal reflexes would cause bilateral responses, not the one-sided weakness described.

items.stem: Rising levels of thyroid hormones (T3 and T4) in the blood exert what effect on the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis?
options: It causes the hypothalamus to release even more TRH in positive feedback
It causes the pituitary to release TSH faster to speed up responses
It inhibits the release of TSH from the anterior pituitary by negative feedback
It stops all hypothalamic regulation of the thyroid permanently
items.rationale: High circulating T3 and T4 feed back negatively on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, lowering TRH and TSH to return hormone levels to normal.
distractor_rationales: This reflects positive feedback; the dominant pattern in endocrine control is negative feedback, as with thyroid hormones.
This confuses direction with speed; endocrine responses are characteristically slower than nervous ones.
Correct: rising thyroid hormone levels act on the hypothalamus and pituitary to reduce TRH and TSH, a classic negative feedback loop.
The pituitary is stimulated by TRH from the hypothalamus, so describing no hypothalamic role is incorrect.

llm_review.issues: Option 3 is correct but focuses on pituitary TSH inhibition; rising T3/T4 also inhibit hypothalamic TRH, which is part of the same negative feedback axis.

items.stem: A patient taking long-term high-dose corticosteroid therapy develops elevated blood glucose. Which hormone class explains this effect?
options: Insulin from the pancreatic beta cells
items.rationale: Chronic glucocorticoid excess (as in Cushing syndrome) raises blood glucose by stimulating glucose production, opposing insulin's effects.
distractor_rationales: Correct: glucocorticoids such as cortisol raise blood glucose during stress, opposing insulin's glucose-lowering effect.
Insulin lowers blood glucose, so long-term excess would cause hypoglycemia, not the hyperglycemia described.
Aldosterone regulates sodium and water balance and is not responsible for stress-related glucose elevation.
Androgens in excess would produce masculinizing effects, not elevated blood glucose.

items.stem: The sodium-potassium pump uses one ATP for each exchange cycle. If a neuron's pumps complete 12 cycles, how many sodium and potassium ions are moved?
items.rationale: Each ATP hydrolyzed drives 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in. For 12 ATP: 12 x 3 = 36 Na+ out and 12 x 2 = 24 K+ in.
distractor_rationales: Each pump restores 3 sodium out and 2 potassium in, so a 1:1 ratio of ions moved would understate the sodium movement.
Reversing the directions would abolish the gradients the pump normally maintains, giving the wrong geometry.
Correct: one ATP pumps 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in; 12 ATP therefore moves 36 Na+ out and 24 K+ in.
Doubling both counts, as if each ATP moved 6 Na+ and 4 K+, doubles the true result.

ap_respiratory.title: Respiratory system and gas exchange
ap_respiratory.intro_markdown: The respiratory system delivers air to the lungs, where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged with the blood. Air travels from the nose or mouth through the pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, and progressively smaller bronchioles to reach the alveoli — thin-walled sacs surrounded by pulmonary capillaries. Gas exchange occurs across this alveolar-capillary membrane by simple diffusion, driven by partial pressure gradients: oxygen moves from alveolar air (high PO2) into deoxygenated blood (low PO2), while carbon dioxide moves from blood into alveolar air. Ventilation is powered by the diaphragm and intercostal muscles; contraction expands the chest, dropping intrapleural and alveolar pressure so air flows in. Most oxygen travels bound to hemoglobin, and most carbon dioxide is carried as bicarbonate. Worked example: blood returning from tissues has a PO2 of about 40 mmHg while alveolar air is about 104 mmHg, so oxygen diffuses into blood until it equilibrates near 100 mmHg.
key_points: Gas exchange occurs only at the alveoli, across a membrane one cell thick.
Inspiration is active: diaphragm contraction enlarges the thorax, lowering alveolar pressure below atmospheric pressure.
O2 and CO2 cross the respiratory membrane by simple diffusion down partial pressure gradients — no ATP required.
CO2, not O2, is the strongest normal driver of ventilation via medullary chemoreceptors sensing pH.
About 70% of CO2 travels as plasma bicarbonate; the Bohr effect (high CO2/H+) shifts the O2-Hb curve right to unload O2 in active tissues.

items.stem: In which structure of the respiratory system does the actual exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide with the blood take place?
items.rationale: Gas exchange occurs only in the respiratory zone. Alveoli have walls one cell thick and are enveloped by capillaries, creating a short diffusion path for O2 and CO2.
distractor_rationales: The trachea is the conducting airway leading to the bronchi, not the gas exchange surface.
The primary bronchi branch from the trachea and deliver air to each lung but do not exchange gases.
Correct. The alveoli are thin-walled sacs wrapped in pulmonary capillaries, forming the respiratory membrane where diffusion occurs.
The larynx contains the vocal cords and conducts air; its walls are far too thick for diffusion.

items.stem: Which statement correctly describes what happens during quiet inspiration?
options: The diaphragm relaxes and pushes air into the lungs.
The diaphragm contracts, flattening downward and pulling air into the lungs.
The diaphragm relaxes, dropping the floor of the thoracic cavity.
The diaphragm is a smooth muscle that contracts automatically for each breath.
items.rationale: Inhaling is an active process: diaphragmatic contraction flattens the dome, increasing thoracic volume and lowering intrapulmonary pressure so air flows in.
distractor_rationales: Contraction flattens the diaphragm, increasing thoracic volume and causing inhalation, not exhalation.
Correct. Diaphragm contraction flattens the dome, enlarging the thoracic cavity; pressure falls below atmospheric and air flows in.
Relaxation of the diaphragm allows it to dome upward, decreasing volume and pushing air out — the reverse of inhalation.
The diaphragm is skeletal muscle, not smooth muscle, and its role is not direct gas exchange.

items.stem: A student inhales quietly. According to Boyle's law, what happens to alveolar (intrapulmonary) pressure and air movement?
options: Alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric pressure, and air flows into the lungs.
Alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric pressure, and air flows into the lungs.
Intrapleural pressure becomes positive, sucking air through the bronchi.
The thoracic cavity shrinks, increasing alveolar pressure.
items.rationale: Inspiration expands the thorax, so alveolar pressure drops below atmospheric pressure and air moves down its pressure gradient into the alveoli.
distractor_rationales: Correct. Boyle's law: expanding the thorax lowers alveolar pressure below atmospheric, creating the gradient for inflow.
Alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric during exhalation, driving air out.
Pressure gradients, not pleural adhesion, move air; pleural pressure is already negative throughout the cycle.
Contraction shrinks the cavity during exhalation; it expands during inspiration.

items.stem: Which statement best describes how oxygen and carbon dioxide move between the alveoli and the pulmonary capillaries?
options: Gases move by active transport using ATP at the alveolar membrane.
Oxygen diffuses into blood, but carbon dioxide is actively pumped into the alveoli.
Gases move by facilitated diffusion through protein channels.
Gases move by simple diffusion from areas of higher to lower partial pressure.
items.rationale: Both O2 and CO2 cross the 0.5-micrometer respiratory membrane by simple diffusion, driven solely by their partial pressure gradients; no cellular energy is spent.
distractor_rationales: Gas movement in the lungs requires no ATP; simple diffusion along partial pressure gradients does the work.
The statement is false, so reversing it cannot be the best answer.
The statement is false; active transport is not used at the respiratory membrane.
Correct. O2 and CO2 cross the alveolar-capillary membrane by simple diffusion, powered by partial pressure differences, not ATP.

items.stem: Which mechanism normally provides the strongest stimulus controlling the rate and depth of breathing in a healthy adult?
options: Falling oxygen levels in the blood directly stimulate the medulla most strongly.
Rising carbon dioxide and falling blood pH stimulate chemoreceptors to increase ventilation.
Low CO2 levels excite peripheral baroreceptors to slow breathing.
Stretch receptors in the alveoli increase the respiratory rate when CO2 rises.
items.rationale: Carbon dioxide is the main chemical driver of ventilation: CO2 crosses into CSF, forms carbonic acid, and the pH drop stimulates medullary chemoreceptors to raise breathing rate and depth.
distractor_rationales: Low oxygen stimulates breathing only weakly in healthy adults; carbon dioxide is the dominant stimulus.
Correct. Rising CO2 lowers blood pH, stimulating central chemoreceptors in the medulla to increase the rate and depth of breathing.
Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies do respond, but the primary drive is the central medullary response to pH, and CO2 is not low.
Baroreceptors regulate blood pressure, not ventilation.

items.stem: What is the primary way carbon dioxide is transported from the tissues to the lungs in the blood?
options: As bicarbonate ions in the plasma
Dissolved directly in the plasma as CO2 gas
Bound to the heme groups of hemoglobin
Carried inside white blood cells as carbonic acid
items.rationale: About 70% of CO2 enters red blood cells, is converted by carbonic anhydrase to carbonic acid, dissociates into bicarbonate, and is transported in plasma; only about 20-25% rides on hemoglobin.
distractor_rationales: Correct. Roughly 70% of CO2 is converted to bicarbonate via carbonic anhydrase in red blood cells, then carried in plasma.
Dissolved CO2 in plasma accounts for only about 5-7% of transported carbon dioxide.
Carbaminohemoglobin carries only about 20-25% of CO2, and CO2 binds the globin portion, not the heme iron.
Most CO2 travels in plasma as bicarbonate, not inside white blood cells.

items.stem: A patient develops pulmonary edema, in which fluid accumulates in the interstitial space between the alveoli and the pulmonary capillaries. Which effect best explains why this patient's arterial oxygen levels fall?
options: The partial pressure difference for oxygen will be reversed at the membrane.
The alveolar membrane will thicken from scar tissue.
The surface area for gas exchange will increase without the fluid.
The diffusion distance will increase, slowing gas exchange according to Fick's law.
items.rationale: Fick's law states diffusion is inversely proportional to membrane thickness. Interstitial fluid lengthens the path oxygen must travel from alveolus to blood, reducing uptake.
distractor_rationales: The alveolar PO2 is unchanged by edema; the problem is the diffusion barrier, not the gradient itself.
Fibrosis thickens the membrane but is not stated here; the scenario describes fluid accumulation.
The partial pressure difference is not reversed; both alveolar and blood PO2 remain as normal.
Correct. Fick's law shows diffusion slows as membrane thickness increases; the fluid adds to the barrier, lengthening the diffusion path for oxygen.

llm_review.issues: Option 4 is correct; however, pulmonary edema hypoxemia also involves V/Q mismatch/shunt, so diffusion distance alone is an incomplete clinical explanation.

items.stem: During exercise, active skeletal muscle produces more carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions. According to the Bohr effect, what happens to the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, and what is the result?
options: The curve shifts left, and hemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly in the tissues.
The curve shifts right, and hemoglobin picks up more oxygen in active tissues.
The curve shifts right, and hemoglobin releases oxygen more readily in active tissues.
The curve shifts left, and hemoglobin cannot load oxygen in the lungs.
items.rationale: The Bohr effect: rising CO2 and H+ in metabolically active tissue decrease hemoglobin's oxygen affinity, shifting the curve right and enhancing oxygen unloading exactly where it is needed.
distractor_rationales: A left shift means increased affinity; CO2 and H+ actually decrease affinity, shifting the curve right, so this is backwards.
Hemoglobin picks up oxygen in the lungs, not in active tissues; the right shift promotes unloading, not uptake.
Correct. CO2 and H+ lower hemoglobin's oxygen affinity (Bohr effect), shifting the curve right so more oxygen unloads in tissues with high metabolic activity.
Oxygen loading in the lungs is not impaired; hemoglobin still fully saturates in the alveoli.

ap_terminology.title: Anatomical position, planes, directional terms, body cavities
ap_terminology.intro_markdown:
Anatomists use a shared vocabulary so descriptions mean the same thing regardless of the body's actual orientation. In **standard anatomical position**, the body is upright, facing forward, arms at the sides, palms and feet facing forward. From this reference, **directional terms** describe locations: superior (toward the head) vs. inferior (toward the feet); anterior/ventral (front) vs. posterior/dorsal (back); medial (toward the midline) vs. lateral (away); proximal (nearer the trunk) vs. distal (farther, used for limbs); superficial vs. deep.

**Planes** are imaginary cuts: the sagittal plane divides left and right (midsagittal splits evenly); the frontal (coronal) plane divides front from back; the transverse (horizontal) plane divides top from bottom.

**Body cavities** house organs: the dorsal cavity holds the brain and spinal cord; the ventral cavity contains the thoracic cavity (heart, lungs) and abdominopelvic cavity (digestive organs, bladder, reproductive organs). The diaphragm separates thoracic from abdominal cavities.

Worked example: The elbow is proximal to the wrist because it lies closer to the shoulder (trunk) when describing the upper limb.
key_points: Anatomical position: upright, facing forward, palms and feet forward — all directional terms assume this pose
Directional pairs: superior/inferior, anterior/posterior, medial/lateral, proximal/distal, superficial/deep
Sagittal = left/right; frontal (coronal) = front/back; transverse = top/bottom
Dorsal cavity = cranial + vertebral; ventral cavity = thoracic + abdominopelvic, separated by the diaphragm
The diaphragm divides the thoracic cavity from the abdominal cavity

items.stem: Which description matches the standard anatomical position?
options: Standing upright, facing forward, palms facing backward
Lying face down with arms at the sides
Standing upright, facing forward, palms and feet facing forward
Seated with arms crossed over the chest
items.rationale: Standard anatomical position is erect, facing forward, arms at sides, palms anterior, feet forward. All directional terms assume this orientation.
distractor_rationales: Palms facing backward is incorrect; in anatomical position the palms face anteriorly, which is why the radius is lateral.
Lying face down is the prone position, not the anatomical position.
Correct: upright, facing forward, arms at sides with palms and feet directed forward.
The body must be upright and facing forward, not seated or sideways.

items.stem: The thorax is ______ to the abdomen.
items.rationale: The thorax is closer to the head than the abdomen, making it superior to the abdomen.
distractor_rationales: Superior means toward the head; the neck lies above the thorax, so the thorax is inferior to the neck.
Correct: superior means toward the head, and the thorax is above the abdomen.
Anterior means toward the front, not toward the head.
Proximal is used only for points along a limb relative to the trunk.

items.stem: A CT scan image shows a horizontal cross-section of the abdomen that separates superior from inferior structures. Which plane produced this view?
items.rationale: A horizontal cut through the waist yields an upper (superior) and lower (inferior) portion, which defines the transverse plane.
distractor_rationales: Correct: the transverse (horizontal) plane divides the body into superior and inferior parts.
The frontal plane divides anterior from posterior.
The sagittal plane divides the body into right and left portions.
The midsagittal plane creates equal right and left halves specifically.

llm_review.issues: Option 4 is a subtype of option 3, creating minor non-independence among distractors.

items.stem: A surgeon makes a vertical cut that separates the chest into front and back portions. Which plane does this cut follow?
items.rationale: The frontal (coronal) plane divides the body into anterior and posterior portions, which is what a vertical front-to-back cut creates.
distractor_rationales: The diaphragm is a landmark, not a body plane.
The midsagittal plane divides left and right halves along the midline.
The transverse plane divides superior from inferior.
Correct: the frontal (coronal) plane separates anterior from posterior.

items.stem: Which term describes the position of the heart relative to the lungs?
items.rationale: The heart sits between the lungs, nearer the body's midline, so it is medial to each lung.
distractor_rationales: Lateral means away from the midline; the heart is medial in the thorax, between the lungs.
Correct: the heart lies between the lungs, closer to the body's midline, so it is medial to each lung.
Anterior describes the front of the body, not a relationship to the lungs.
The heart is within the thoracic cavity, so it is not external to it.

llm_review.issues: Option 3 is a plausible but incorrect distractor; the heart is medial to the lungs, not anterior to them.

items.stem: Which structure separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominal cavity?
items.rationale: The dome-shaped diaphragm forms the floor of the thoracic cavity and the roof of the abdominal cavity, separating them.
distractor_rationales: Correct: the diaphragm is the muscular partition between the thoracic and abdominal cavities.
The mediastinum is the central compartment of the thoracic cavity, not a cavity separator.
The peritoneum is the serous membrane lining the abdominal cavity, not a divider between cavities.
The pleura is the membrane around the lungs, located within the thoracic cavity.

items.stem: A patient has a wound on the leg. Which term correctly completes this statement: 'The knee is ______ to the ankle.'
items.rationale: Proximal means nearer the point of attachment (trunk). The knee attaches closer to the hip than the ankle does, so the ankle is distal to the knee and the knee is proximal to the ankle; between knee and ankle, the knee is proximal.
distractor_rationales: The knee is farther from the trunk than the ankle, so it is distal to the ankle, not proximal.
Superior/inferior are used for trunk or whole-body relationships, not along the limbs.

Correct: the ankle is closer to the trunk along the lower limb than the knee, making it proximal to the knee... the ankle lies nearer the trunk, so the knee is distal to the ankle and the ankle is proximal to the toes; here the knee is farther from the trunk than the ankle, so it is distal to the ankle.
Distal is reversed; the knee is farther from the hip (trunk) than the ankle is not the comparison asked—here the ankle is proximal to the toes only.

items.stem: The spinal cord is located within which body cavity arrangement?
options: The dorsal cavity containing the thoracic cavity
The ventral cavity containing the abdominal cavity
The dorsal cavity containing the vertebral canal
items.rationale: The spinal cord lies in the vertebral canal, which, with the cranial cavity, makes up the dorsal body cavity.
distractor_rationales: The dorsal body cavity contains the cranial and vertebral (spinal) cavities, not the thoracic cavity.
The abdominal cavity contains digestive organs; the spinal cord is in the vertebral canal, part of the dorsal cavity.
The abdominopelvic cavity is ventral and contains digestive, urinary, and reproductive organs, not the spinal cord.
Correct: the vertebral canal, within the dorsal body cavity, houses the spinal cord.

llm_review.issues: Stem wording 'body cavity arrangement' is awkward; option 1 is anatomically implausible and weakens distractor quality.

grammar_agreement.title: Subject-verb and pronoun-antecedent agreement
grammar_agreement.intro_markdown: Agreement means matching two parts of a sentence in number: a verb must agree with its true subject, and a pronoun must agree with its antecedent (the word it replaces). The trap on exams is that extra words sit between the subject and the verb. In "The list of medications is long," the subject is "list," not "medications," so the verb is singular. Ignore prepositional phrases when checking agreement. A few patterns to memorize: subjects joined by "and" usually take a plural verb; with "either/or" and "neither/nor," the verb agrees with the subject closer to it; indefinite pronouns such as "each," "every," and "everyone" are singular; and collective nouns like "staff" or "team" are treated as singular in formal writing. For pronouns, find the antecedent first, then match its number exactly.
key_points: Cross out prepositional phrases to find the true subject before choosing a verb.
Subjects joined by 'and' are plural; with 'either/or' and 'neither/nor,' agree with the nearer subject.
'Each,' 'every,' and 'everyone' are singular and take singular verbs and pronouns.
Collective nouns such as 'staff' and 'team' are singular in formal writing.
A pronoun must match its antecedent in number, even when other nouns intervene.

items.stem: The list of medications ______ on the chart at the bedside.
items.rationale: The subject is the singular noun 'list'; 'of medications' is a prepositional phrase and never controls the verb. Singular subject takes the singular verb 'is listed.'
distractor_rationales: This is attraction error: the verb was made plural to match 'medications' inside the prepositional phrase, not the true subject 'list.'
Correct: the true subject is the singular noun 'list,' so it takes the singular verb 'is listed.'
'Were' is plural and also past tense, but the sentence calls for the singular present tense verb.
This plural verb was pulled from 'medications' and adds an unnecessary perfect tense.

items.stem: Heart rate and respiratory rate ______ at least every four hours.
items.rationale: Two subjects joined by 'and' (heart rate and respiratory rate) form a plural compound subject, which requires the plural verb 'are recorded.'
distractor_rationales: 'Is' is singular, but a compound subject joined by 'and' is plural.
'Was' is both singular and past tense; neither fits a compound present-tense subject.
Correct: 'Heart rate and respiratory rate' is a compound subject joined by 'and,' so it takes the plural verb 'are recorded.'
'Has been recorded' is singular and perfect tense; the plural compound subject needs a plural present-tense verb.

items.stem: Either the residents or their families ______ to the care conference.
items.rationale: In 'either/or' and 'neither/nor' constructions, the verb agrees with the subject closest to it. 'Families' is plural, so the plural verb 'are invited' is correct.
distractor_rationales: Correct: with 'either/or,' the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it; 'families' is plural, so 'are invited' is correct.
'Is' would agree only with the singular 'residents,' which is the farther subject and does not control the verb.
'Was' is both singular and past tense, so it fails on number and tense.
'Will be inviting' changes the meaning; the families receive the invitation rather than give it.

items.stem: Each of the patients ______ an identification bracelet before transfer.
items.rationale: The subject is the indefinite pronoun 'each,' which is always singular even though 'patients' is plural. The object of a prepositional phrase never controls the verb, so the singular 'wears' is correct.
distractor_rationales: 'Wear' is plural; the true subject 'each' is singular, so the verb must be singular.
'Are wearing' matches 'patients' inside the phrase, but the object of 'of' never controls the verb.
'Have worn' is plural and perfect tense; neither matches the singular subject 'each.'
Correct: 'Each' is a singular indefinite pronoun, so it takes the singular verb 'wears.'

items.stem: Every patient must update ______ contact information before the appointment.
items.rationale: The antecedent 'every patient' is singular; 'every' always creates a singular reference. Formal written English requires the singular pronoun 'his or her' to match.
distractor_rationales: 'Their' is plural, but 'every patient' is a singular antecedent in formal written English.
Correct: the singular antecedent 'every patient' takes the singular pronoun 'his or her' in formal grammar.
'Them' is plural and also an object pronoun, so it fails to agree and is the wrong case.
'Its' is singular but refers to nonhuman antecedents; a patient is a person, not a thing.

items.stem: The nursing staff ______ required to attend the in-service on Friday.
items.rationale: 'Staff' is a collective noun treated as singular in formal writing because the group acts as one unit here, so it takes the singular verb 'is required.'
distractor_rationales: Correct: 'staff' is a collective noun acting as one unit, so it takes the singular verb 'is required.'
'Are' treats the staff as separate individuals; formal writing keeps the collective noun singular.
'Were being' is plural and awkwardly passive; the singular present-tense verb is needed.
'Have been' is plural, matching the writers' sense of many employees rather than one unit.

items.stem: The results of the urinalysis ______ within normal limits.
items.rationale: The true subject is the plural noun 'results'; 'of the urinalysis' is only a prepositional phrase. A plural subject takes the plural verb 'were.'
distractor_rationales: 'Was' is singular; it was likely pulled from the idea of one test rather than the plural subject 'results.'
'Is' is singular and present tense; the subject is plural and the context is past.
Correct: the subject 'results' is plural, so it takes the plural past-tense verb 'were.'
'Has been' is singular; it also mismatches the plural 'results.'

items.stem: Neither the surgeon nor the technicians have finished ______ reports.
items.rationale: In a 'neither/nor' construction, both the verb and pronoun agree with the nearer antecedent. 'Technicians' is plural, matching the plural verb 'have' and the pronoun 'their.'
distractor_rationales: 'His or her' is singular, but the nearer antecedent 'technicians' is plural and controls the pronoun.
'His' is singular and assumes all technicians are male; it fails to agree with the plural antecedent.
'Its' refers to nonhuman antecedents and is singular; people cannot be called 'its.'
Correct: with 'neither/nor,' the pronoun agrees with the nearer antecedent, the plural 'technicians,' so 'their' is correct.

grammar_confused_words.title: Commonly confused words (affect/effect, their/there, lie/lay)
grammar_confused_words.intro_markdown: Many spelling mix-ups involve short words that sound alike. "Affect" is usually a verb meaning to influence: "Stress can affect blood pressure." "Effect" is usually a noun meaning a result: "The medication had a soothing effect." "Their" shows possession, "there" points to a place, and "they're" is short for "they are." "Lie" means to recline and takes no object ("I lie down"), while "lay" means to put something down and takes an object ("I lay the chart on the desk"). A quick check: if you can substitute a form of "to place" and the sentence still works, use "lay." If you can substitute "to recline," use "lie."
key_points: Affect is usually a verb meaning to influence; effect is usually a noun meaning a result.
Their shows possession, there indicates a place, and they're is the contraction of they are.
Lie means to recline and takes no object; lay means to put something down and takes an object.
The past tense of lie is lay; the past tense of lay is laid.
Affect can be a noun in psychology (observable mood), and effect can be a verb meaning to bring about, but these uses are less common.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: The nurse explained that low potassium levels can ______ a patient's heart rhythm.
options: Lack of sleep can effect a patient's ability to heal.
Lack of sleep can affect a patient's ability to heal.
Lack of sleep can affectation a patient's ability to heal.
Lack of sleep can effects a patient's ability to heal.
items.rationale: After the modal verb 'can,' a main verb is needed. 'Affect' is the verb meaning 'to influence,' so it correctly completes the sentence.
distractor_rationales: Uses the noun form where the sentence needs the verb meaning 'to influence.'
Correct: 'affect' is the verb meaning 'to influence,' which fits after the modal 'can.'
Uses the noun form where the verb is required.
Not a standard word in this context; it is a misspelling of the verb form.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: The new nursing students left the orientation packets over ______.
options: The new students were assigned rooms over they're.
The new students were assigned rooms over their.
The new students were assigned rooms over there.
The new students were assigned rooms over theirs.
items.rationale: The sentence needs a word pointing to a location. 'There' is the adverb of place; 'their' is possessive and 'they're' means 'they are.'
distractor_rationales: 'They're' means 'they are,' which does not fit before 'assigned rooms.'
'Their' is possessive and would wrongly make 'rooms' belong to the students.
Correct: 'there' is the adverb pointing to a location.
'Theirs' is a standalone pronoun and cannot modify a noun.

llm_review.issues: Stem and options mismatch: the stem asks to complete 'left the orientation packets over ____,' but the options complete a different sentence about assigned rooms. Option 3 remains the only grammatically correct homophone choice.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: Every staff member should label ______ supplies before the shift begins.
options: Every staff member should label their supplies before the shift begins.
Every staff member should label there supplies before the shift begins.
Every staff member should label they're supplies before the shift begins.
Every staff member should label theirs supplies before the shift begins.
items.rationale: The blank requires a possessive adjective modifying 'supplies.' 'Their' shows ownership; 'there' is a place word and 'they're' means 'they are.'
distractor_rationales: Correct: 'their' is the possessive form showing the supplies belong to the staff members.
'There' indicates place, not possession, and does not fit before a noun.
'They're' means 'they are,' which creates a nonsensical sentence.
'Theirs' stands alone and cannot modify the noun 'supplies.'

items.stem: Choose the correct verb form: The aide ______ the safety bars up before transferring the patient.
options: The aide lie the safety bars up before transferring the patient.
The aide lays the safety bars up before transferring the patient.
The aide lain the safety bars up before transferring the patient.
The aide laid the safety bars up before transferring the patient.
items.rationale: 'Lay' means to put something down and takes an object ('safety bars'). Its past tense is 'laid,' which fits this past-tense sentence.
distractor_rationales: 'Lie' takes no object; 'safety bars' would be left without a verb acting on it.
'Lays' is present tense, but the sentence needs the past-tense verb that takes an object.
'Lain' is the past participle of 'lie' and cannot take the object 'safety bars.'
Correct: 'laid' is the past tense of 'lay,' the verb meaning 'to put something down,' and takes the object 'safety bars.'

items.stem: Choose the correct word: The physician reviewed the possible side ______ of the new antibiotic before obtaining the patient's consent.
options: The charge nurse documented the patient's affect after administering the new medication.
The charge nurse documented the effects of the new medication on the patient.
The charge nurse documented the patient's affects after the new medication.
The charge nurse documented the patient's effecting after the new medication.
items.rationale: The sentence needs the plural noun meaning 'results,' which is 'effects.' 'Affect' as a noun refers to observable mood or emotional expression, not outcomes.
distractor_rationales: Uses the verb form where the noun 'result' is required.
'Effects' as a verb means 'brings about,' which would need a direct object like 'change,' not an adjective phrase.
Correct: 'effects' is the plural noun meaning 'results' or 'outcomes.'
Combines the noun form with a verb ending, creating a grammatically impossible form.

items.stem: Choose the correct verb form: After the procedure, the patient ______ in the recovery room for an hour.
options: After the procedure, the patient lain in the recovery room for an hour.
After the procedure, the patient lay in the recovery room for an hour.
After the procedure, the patient laid in the recovery room for an hour.
After the procedure, the patient laying in the recovery room for an hour.
items.rationale: 'Lie' (to recline) has the past tense 'lay.' The patient reclines, and no object follows, so 'lay' is correct here even though it looks like the present of another verb.
distractor_rationales: Reverses the tenses: 'lain' is for 'lie' and 'lay' is present tense for 'lay.'
Correct: 'lay' is the past tense of 'lie' (to recline), which needs no object.
Uses the past tense of 'lay,' which requires an object.
Adds an '-ing' ending, which does not fit with 'for an hour.'

items.stem: Choose the correct sentence with both words used properly.
options: The assessment noted that the patient's affect was flat and that the medication's effects appeared within thirty minutes.
The assessment noted that the patient's effect was flat and that the medication's affects appeared within thirty minutes.
The assessment noted that the patient's affects were flat and that the medication's effecting appeared within thirty minutes.
The assessment noted that the patient's affect was flat and that the medication's affecting appeared within thirty minutes.
items.rationale: 'Affect' as a noun means observable emotional expression ('flat affect'). 'Effects' as a plural noun means results, which fits the medication's outcomes.
distractor_rationales: Correct: 'affect' (noun) means observable emotional expression, and 'effects' (noun) means results.
Uses 'effect,' which does not describe observable emotional expression.
'Affects' is a verb, not the noun needed after 'flat.'
'Affect' cannot describe emotional expression, and 'affecting' is a verb form.

items.stem: Choose the sentence in which all three commonly confused words are used correctly.
options: The patient was lying quietly when the nurse placed their call light over there.
The patient was laying quietly when the nurse placed they're call light over there.
The patient was lying quietly when the nurse placed there call light over their.
The patient was lying quietly when the nurse placed their call light over there.
items.rationale: 'Lying' correctly describes reclining without an object; 'their' shows the call light belongs to the patient; 'there' points to the location where it was placed.
distractor_rationales: 'Lying' fits the patient but 'there' is a place word and cannot modify 'call light.'
'Laying' would wrongly take the patient as an object, and 'they're' means 'they are.'
'Lying' fits, but 'their' would mean the call light belongs to the nurses rather than identifying it.
Correct: 'lying' (reclining, no object), 'their' (possessive, belonging to the patient), and 'there' (place) all fit.

grammar_parts_of_speech.title: Parts of speech
grammar_parts_of_speech.intro_markdown: Every word in an English sentence belongs to a part of speech, a category describing its job rather than its meaning. The eight main categories are noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction, and interjection. Nouns name people, places, things, or ideas; pronouns replace nouns; verbs show action or link subject to description; adjectives modify nouns; adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs; prepositions begin phrases showing relationships such as location or time; conjunctions join words or clauses; interjections express emotion. To classify a word, test its function in the sentence. Consider this worked example: in "The tired aide quickly entered the quiet ward," "aide" and "ward" are nouns, "tired" and "quiet" are adjectives, "entered" is a verb, and "quickly" is an adverb telling how the entering happened. One word can shift categories, so always analyze the role it plays in the specific sentence. Identifying parts of speech builds the foundation for spotting agreement, case, and modification errors on the exam.
key_points: Classify words by function in the sentence, not by meaning alone.
Adjectives modify nouns; adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs.
Subject pronouns (I, he) act in subjects; object pronouns (me, him) receive action.
A gerund is an -ing verb form used as a noun; the same form used to modify is a participle.
Prepositions begin phrases of relationship (location, time, direction); conjunctions join words or clauses.

items.stem: Which word in the following sentence is a noun? The nurse recorded the patient's temperature carefully.
items.rationale: A noun names a person, place, thing, or idea. "Temperature" names a thing and serves as the object of the verb "recorded."
distractor_rationales: The is an article, a special type of adjective, not a noun.
Recorded is the action verb of the sentence, showing what the nurse did.
Carefully is an adverb modifying the verb recorded, describing how the action was done.
Temperature names a thing and serves as the direct object of the verb recorded.

items.stem: Which word in the following sentence is a verb? The pharmacist reviewed the chart before the shift ended.
items.rationale: A verb expresses action or state of being. "Reviewed" is the action the pharmacist performed, so it is the verb of the sentence.
distractor_rationales: Reviewed expresses the action performed by the subject, making it the verb.
Pharmacist is a noun naming the person who performs the action.
Before is a preposition here, beginning the phrase before the shift.
Chart is a noun naming the object being reviewed.

items.stem: Which word in the following sentence is an adverb? The aide quietly opened the heavy door.
items.rationale: An adverb modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb. "Quietly" modifies the verb "opened," telling how the opening was done.
distractor_rationales: Quiet is an adjective describing the aide, but the sentence uses quietly to describe the action, not the noun.
Heavy is an adjective describing the noun door.
Door is a noun naming the object being opened.
Quietly modifies the verb opened, telling how the action was performed, which is the role of an adverb.

llm_review.issues: Option 1, 'quiet,' is not actually present in the sentence, making it an invalid distractor for a question asking which word in the sentence is an adverb.

items.stem: Which pronoun correctly completes the sentence? The director thanked the volunteer and ____ for organizing the supply closet.
items.rationale: The pronoun is part of the compound object of "thanked." Object position requires an object pronoun, so "her" is correct.
distractor_rationales: She is a subject pronoun and cannot serve as the object of the verb thanked.
Her is the object form, correctly receiving the action of the verb thanked, even when paired with a named person.
Herself is a reflexive pronoun used only when the subject acts upon itself, which does not fit here.
Hers is a possessive pronoun showing ownership, not an object receiving the action.

items.stem: Which word in the following sentence functions as a preposition? The supply cart was parked beside the elevator.
items.rationale: A preposition begins a phrase showing a relationship such as location or time. "Beside" begins the phrase "beside the elevator" and tells where the cart was parked.
distractor_rationales: Parked is the verb of the sentence, expressing the action performed on the cart.
The is an article functioning as an adjective, not a preposition.
Beside begins the prepositional phrase beside the elevator, showing the relationship of location between the cart and the elevator.
Elevator is the object of the preposition, a noun, not the preposition itself.

items.stem: Which word in the following sentence is a linking verb? The patient's skin remained warm throughout the evening.
items.rationale: A linking verb connects the subject to a word that describes it. "Remained" links the subject "skin" to the predicate adjective "warm" rather than showing action.
distractor_rationales: Remained is a linking verb connecting the subject skin to the predicate adjective warm.
Warm is a predicate adjective describing the subject after the linking verb.
Skin is the subject noun being described.
Evening is a noun telling when, part of the adverbial prepositional phrase.

items.stem: Which word in the following sentence functions as a noun? Charting accurately takes practice.
items.rationale: A gerund is an -ing form used as a noun. "Charting" acts as the subject of the sentence, so it functions as a noun despite its verb form.
distractor_rationales: Takes is the main verb of the sentence, showing what charting does.
Accurately is an adverb modifying the gerund charting.
Practice is a noun serving as the direct object of the gerund phrase, not the gerund itself.
Charting is a gerund, an -ing verb form functioning as a noun, because it serves as the subject of the verb takes.

items.stem: Which word in the following sentence functions as a relative pronoun? The student who completed the practicum received a certificate.
items.rationale: A relative pronoun introduces a dependent clause and refers to a noun. "Who" begins the clause "who completed the practicum" and stands for "student."
distractor_rationales: The is an article functioning as an adjective modifying student.
Who is a relative pronoun introducing the clause who completed the practicum and referring back to student.
Completed is the verb of the relative clause describing the student.
Received is the main verb of the sentence, showing what the student did.

llm_review.issues: Distractors are different parts of speech and do not compete with the relative pronoun, making the item very easy.

grammar_punctuation.title: Punctuation and sentence structure
grammar_punctuation.intro_markdown: Punctuation marks do the traffic control work of English sentences. A period ends a complete sentence; a comma joins clauses only when paired with a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so). A semicolon joins two complete sentences without a conjunction. Apostrophes show possession or contraction, never simple plurals. Watch for fragments (incomplete thoughts), run-ons (fused sentences), and comma splices (two sentences joined by only a comma). Example: "The nurse charted the vitals; they were stable." The semicolon correctly joins two complete thoughts.
key_points: Commas join independent clauses only with a coordinating conjunction (and, but, or, so, yet, for, nor).
Semicolons join two independent clauses without a conjunction.
A comma alone between two complete sentences is a comma splice—an error.
Apostrophes show possession or contractions, never simple plurals.
Introductory dependent clauses are followed by a comma; nonessential clauses take paired commas.

items.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The aide asked. Did the patient eat breakfast?
The aide asked, did the patient eat breakfast?
The aide asked; did the patient eat breakfast?
The aide asked, did the patient eat breakfast!
items.rationale: A direct question introduced by a comma inside a sentence ends with a question mark. Only the comma before it is needed to set it off.
distractor_rationales: A period cannot replace the question mark; a direct question needs a question mark regardless of sentence position.
Correct: a direct question embedded in a sentence is set off by a comma and ends with a question mark.
A semicolon separates complete sentences; it cannot introduce a direct question.
An exclamation point signals strong emotion, which the sentence does not express.

items.stem: Which sentence uses a comma correctly?
options: The shift ended, the nurse finished her notes.
The shift ended. And reviewed the chart one last time.
The shift ended, but the nurse reviewed the chart one last time.
The shift ended but, the nurse reviewed the chart one last time.
items.rationale: A comma before a coordinating conjunction (but) correctly joins two independent clauses. The comma must come before the conjunction, not after it.
distractor_rationales: A comma splice joins two complete sentences with only a comma, which is incorrect.
A period creates a fragment because 'and reviewed the chart' has no subject and cannot stand alone.
Correct: the comma before the conjunction 'but' properly joins two complete sentences.
No punctuation before the coordinating conjunction creates a run-on (fused) sentence.

items.stem: Which sentence punctuates the introductory clause correctly?
options: After the patient stabilized, the nurse left the room.
After the patient, stabilized the nurse left the room.
After the patient stabilized; the nurse left the room.
After the patient stabilized the nurse left the room.
items.rationale: An introductory dependent clause is followed by a comma. 'After the patient stabilized' cannot stand alone, so it must be separated from the main clause.
distractor_rationales: Correct: 'after the patient stabilized' is an introductory dependent clause and needs a comma after it.
The comma incorrectly separates the clause from its verb; introductory phrases take a comma after, not before.
Semicolons cannot attach a dependent clause to the main clause.
Dependent introductory clauses require a comma; omitting it is an error.

llm_review.issues: Option 2 is an implausible distractor; item is otherwise straightforward.

items.stem: Which sentence uses apostrophes correctly?
options: The unit filed three report's for the incident.
The unit filed three report for the incident.
